passages.text: ISRO executes the Indian Space Programme through centers with distinct roles: launch vehicles are built at the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC) in Thiruvananthapuram; satellites are designed and developed at the U R Rao Satellite Centre (URSC) in Bengaluru; integration and launching take place at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC) in Sriharikota; liquid and cryogenic propulsion stages are developed at the Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC) at Valiamala and Bengaluru; satellite sensors and applications are developed at the Space Applications Centre (SAC) in Ahmedabad; and remote-sensing data reception and dissemination are handled by the National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC) in Hyderabad. The chairman of ISRO also serves as secretary of DOS and chairman of the Space Commission, the apex body that formulates policy for the Indian space program.
passages.title: ISRO

passages.text: ISRO (Indian Space Research Organisation) is the space agency of India, responsible for developing launch vehicles, satellites, and space applications for national development, and for the country's planetary exploration and human spaceflight programs. It is a major constituent of the Department of Space (DOS) of the Government of India and has its headquarters in Bengaluru.
passages.title: ISRO

passages.text: ISRO's satellite fleet supports telecommunications, television broadcasting, radio networking, and meteorology, with transponders in C-band, Extended C-band, Ku-band, and S-band serving users such as Doordarshan, All India Radio, and banking institutions. Societal programs include telemedicine, begun as a 2001 pilot linking a Chennai hospital with a rural clinic in Andhra Pradesh, tele-education through the dedicated EDUSAT satellite, and the Disaster Management Support program, whose decision center at NRSC monitors floods, cyclones, landslides, earthquakes, and forest fires. India is a member of the international COSPAS-SARSAT program, operating two local user terminals and the Indian Mission Control Centre in Bengaluru for distress alerting. The GAGAN satellite-based augmentation system, certified for civil aviation enroute and precision-approach services, and the NavIC regional navigation constellation provide positioning services over the region.

The mission consisted of a Vikram lander, a Pragyan rover, and a propulsion module, and was designed to demonstrate end-to-end capability in safe landing and roving on the lunar surface.
passages.title: Chandrayaan-3 (चन्द्रयान-३)

passages.text: The lander touched down on the lunar surface at 6:04 p.m. local time on 23 August 2023, at the Shiv Shakti point in the southern high latitudes of the Moon's near side. During descent the lander briefly entered hover mode at 850 m above the surface while it searched for a clear parking spot. NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter imaged the landing site five days later, showing the lander's dark shadow against a bright halo produced by the rocket plume interacting with the fine-grained regolith.
passages.title: Chandrayaan-3 (चन्द्रयान-३)

passages.text: Elemental composition. The LIBS instrument made the first-ever in-situ measurements of the elemental composition of the lunar surface near the south pole, confirming the presence of sulfur unambiguously, something not feasible with orbiter instruments. Preliminary analyses also identified aluminum, calcium, iron, chromium, and titanium, with further measurements revealing manganese, silicon, and oxygen. APXS measurements of the soil at the landing site provided evidence supporting the Lunar Magma Ocean hypothesis, which predicts that the primordial lunar crust formed by flotation of lighter anorthite plagioclase, while also detecting magnesium-rich minerals suggesting material ejected from deeper layers during the South Pole-Aitken basin impact. A 2024 analysis in Nature described these as the first measurements of soil composition near the Moon's south pole, offering further evidence that the lunar surface was entirely molten shortly after the Moon formed.
